steps.prompt: You have $3$ shirts, $4$ pairs of trousers and $2$ pairs of shoes. How many different outfits can you make? Do you add or multiply?

cards.title: Choices in a row multiply
cards.body: If a task is made of steps, and step one can be done in $a$ ways, step two in $b$ ways, and so on, then the whole task can be done in $a \times b \times \cdots$ ways. Use "and" to multiply (a shirt AND trousers). Use "or" to add (a starter OR a dessert).

cards.title: Worked example: codes
cards.problem: A code is two letters (A to Z) followed by three digits ($0$ to $9$). How many codes are possible?

steps.text: The two letters can be chosen in $26 \times 26 = 676$ ways.
The three digits can be chosen in $10 \times 10 \times 10 = 1000$ ways, so there are $676 \times 1000 = 676{,}000$ codes.

cards.title: Restrictions first
cards.body: Fill the most restricted spot first. For a three-digit number, the first digit can't be $0$ ($9$ choices). If the digits must all be different, each later spot has one fewer choice. If the number must be even, decide the last digit early.

cards.title: Worked example: different digits
cards.problem: How many three-digit numbers have all three digits different?

steps.text: The first digit can be $1$ to $9$: $9$ choices.

try.prompt: How many choices are there for the first digit?

steps.text: The second digit can be any digit except the first ($9$ choices, now $0$ is allowed), and the third any except those two ($8$). So $9 \times 9 \times 8 = 648$.

try.prompt: How many three-digit numbers have all digits different?

cards.title: The common trap: adding instead of multiplying
cards.body: $3$ shirts and $4$ trousers make $3 \times 4 = 12$ outfits, not $7$. And handle the restrictions (no leading $0$, no repeats, even or odd) before the free spots, or the counts change under you.

prompts: How do you decide whether to add or to multiply in a counting problem?
